segments.t: korTTY can open a KTPH000localKTPH001 control socket so that a script or a coding agent running on the same computer can list your windows, read what a terminal pane is showing and type into it. It is the machine-facing twin of what you do with the mouse and the keyboard: nothing it can do is something you could not do yourself in an open pane.

It is KTPH000off by defaultKTPH001 and has to be switched on per installation under KTPH002Settings › Terminal › Control APIKTPH003. Nothing is reachable over the network at any point, and no other user of the same computer can connect.

While the Control API is on, any program running under your user account on this computer can read every open pane — local shells and SSH sessions alike — and type anything into them, including pressing KTPH001KTPH000KTPH002. That is the same power as sitting at your keyboard. Switch it on when you want a coding agent or a script to drive korTTY, and off again when you do not.
Open KTPH000Settings › TerminalKTPH001 and scroll to KTPH002Control APIKTPH003.
Tick KTPH000Allow a local program to read and control this korTTYKTPH001.
Save. The status line underneath tells you what happened right away — no restart is needed.
The checkbox is unticked, or korTTY has shut the listener down.
Enterprise policy denies the KTPH000 feature; the checkbox is locked.
A listener is up and KTPH000 has been written. The text names the socket or the loopback port.
The listener refused to start. The most common reason is that another korTTY already owns the socket; the text says which.
Unticking the box stops the listener and deletes the socket immediately.
Two more switches under the status line belong to KTPH001MCP clientsKTPH002, such as KTPH003KTPH000KTPH004, and both are off by default:
Serves clients that declare themselves MCP clients, with the read-only method list, masked output and capped reads described below.
Also offers such clients KTPH000, KTPH001 and KTPH002. korTTY still asks you before every write. It can only be changed while KTPH003MCP serverKTPH004 is ticked.

Both switches are greyed out while the Control API checkbox is unticked, with the hint KTPH002Tick the Control API above to use the MCP server.KTPH003; they keep their values and take effect again when you tick the Control API. When the enterprise policy denies KTPH000 or KTPH001, both are unticked and locked, with the hint KTPH004Your organization does not allow the MCP server.KTPH005 Saving with either switch off also drops every "allow for this pane in this session" answer, so switching the write tools on again later asks afresh.

Everything the API owns lives in its own directory, KTPH000, created with owner-only permissions (KTPH001) KTPH002beforeKTPH003 anything binds. The directory, not the socket file, is the real protection: a socket inode is created with the process umask, which on most systems is world-readable.
A unix domain socket at KTPH000
TCP on KTPH000 with an operating-system-assigned port
A client finds the endpoint by reading KTPH000 (mode KTPH001):

The file is written KTPH000lastKTPH001, after the listener is bound, so its existence always implies a reachable endpoint and a readable token. korTTY deletes it, and the socket, when the API is switched off and when the application exits.

The token is 32 random bytes, regenerated on every start, and is required on KTPH000bothKTPH001 transports. On Linux and macOS the owner-only directory is the primary control and the token is defence in depth — against a loosened umask, a shared or network-mounted home directory, or a backup that copied the directory somewhere readable. On Windows it is the only control. It is never logged, never echoed in an error message, never passed on a command line and never shown in a notification: the legitimate client reads it from the file, which is the whole point.

The protocol is newline-delimited JSON-RPC 2.0 — exactly one JSON object per line, UTF-8, at most 1 MiB per line. The first request on a connection must be KTPH000; anything else, and the connection is closed. One failed token closes the connection too.

Requests on one connection are executed KTPH000one at a timeKTPH001: the next line is read only after the previous answer has been queued. A client that needs a long wait and concurrent calls opens a second connection — up to eight at once.

Rather than duplicating the method list here, ask korTTY: KTPH000 returns the full machine-readable surface — every method with its parameters, result shape, errors, CLI equivalent and a worked example, plus the key vocabulary, the error table and the limits. The parameters, results, errors and limits are generated from the same declarations the dispatcher registers, so they cannot drift from the implementation; each KTPH001 line is a command the shipped KTPH002 is tested to accept for that very method.
Push notifications when a coding agent changes state.
Enumerate the windows and tabs, bring one to the front, and open a saved connection in a new tab.
KTPH000, KTPH001, KTPH002, KTPH003, KTPH004, KTPH005, KTPH006, KTPH007, KTPH008, KTPH009, KTPH010, KTPH011
Read a pane, type into it, wait for output, split a local shell, close a split, or find the pane a script runs in from its process ids (KTPH000).
KTPH000, KTPH001, KTPH002, KTPH003, KTPH004, KTPH005, KTPH006, KTPH007
Work with the coding agents korTTY has detected — see KTPH000Coding agentsKTPH001.

The title KTPH000 reports for a terminal tab is its name without the coding-agent glyph, the group prefix or the KTPH001 suffix: the name you gave it with KTPH002Rename TabKTPH003, otherwise the KTPH004title its shell setKTPH005, otherwise the connection's name. The shell's title is chosen by the server, so a client that needs to know which host a tab is connected to should not rely on the title alone. Renaming stays with you in the user interface.

KTPH000 and KTPH001 report each pane's KTPH002, which is KTPH003, KTPH004, KTPH005 or KTPH006 (a sandbox was asked for but is not active), and whether its tab is KTPH007; see KTPH008Session isolationKTPH009.

KTPH000 opens a saved or teamwork connection — by its id, or by its name as the Connection Manager shows it — in a new tab of the focused window (or of KTPH001), with KTPH002 (KTPH003, KTPH004 or KTPH005) in place of the connection's own KTPH012session isolationKTPH013 and KTPH006 for an KTPH014incognito sessionKTPH015. A name two connections share is refused with KTPH007 and their ids, an unknown one with KTPH008. The organization's policy still applies: a blocked server, an isolation below KTPH009 or an incognito session the policy forbids is refused with KTPH010, and a teamwork connection can only be made stricter. korTTY never waits for a question while the call is open: when signing in needs a password, a temporary key or the vault unlocked, the answer is KTPH011 without a tab, and korTTY asks you and opens the tab afterwards. MCP clients cannot call it.

KTPH000 and KTPH001 are KTPH003reservedKTPH004: they answer a definite "not implemented in this version" rather than an unknown-method error, and they are listed as reserved in KTPH002, so a client can tell "korTTY will never do this for you" apart from "you spelled it wrong".
The window's life. It is a counter, not a position, so closing another window never renumbers it.

Every parameter called KTPH000 also accepts a bare tab id, meaning that tab's focused pane, and the alias KTPH001, meaning the pane you are looking at. A bare KTPH002windowKTPH003 id where a pane is expected is refused as ambiguous rather than guessed at — a window usually holds several panes, and picking one silently is how a script types into the wrong terminal.

Ids are minted per korTTY run. Every reply that carries ids also carries the KTPH000 of the running korTTY, and every mutating method accepts an optional KTPH001 parameter: when it does not match, the call fails with KTPH002 instead of writing into whatever pane inherited the id. Re-enumerate whenever KTPH003 changes.

KTPH000 has three modes, and KTPH001 is the default. KTPH002 returns the live screen, including the alternate buffer, right-trimmed. KTPH003 returns the scrollback plus the screen, read under a single buffer lock, newest KTPH004 rows (200 by default). KTPH005 returns what korTTY's coding-agent detector last published for the pane — the detector is never re-run for a request.

KTPH000 blocks until a regular expression or a literal string appears, polling the pane. Output that appears and scrolls away inside a single poll window can be missed in KTPH001 mode; the default KTPH002 mode also searches the scrollback and does not have that gap.

KTPH000, KTPH001 and the single-character keys of KTPH002 are encoded in the pane's KTPH007character encodingKTPH008, so they arrive as the bytes the same keystrokes would produce: an SSH pane set to ISO-8859-1 receives KTPH003 as the single byte KTPH004, not as UTF-8. A character that encoding cannot represent is sent as KTPH005. The KTPH006 methods always send UTF-8, which is what the coding agents read.

When KTPH000 wraps its text in bracketed paste — KTPH001 is KTPH002, or KTPH003 found several lines and a pane that enabled it — korTTY first removes any bracketed-paste markers from the text itself (KTPH004, KTPH005 and their 8-bit forms, which start with the single KTPH006 byte KTPH007 — in a Windows-1252 pane that is the character KTPH008), so the text cannot end the paste early and have its remaining lines run as typed commands. An unbracketed write, which includes every KTPH009, keeps such markers. KTPH010 and the prompt of KTPH011 always remove them, bracketed or not.

KTPH000 works KTPH002onlyKTPH003 on a pane whose tab is a local shell. Anything else is refused with KTPH001. The new shell is started without any dialog, so a script never ends up waiting on a window it cannot see; a split that would need a new connection needs a human, and is not offered.

KTPH000 refuses a tab's KTPH001lastKTPH002 pane. Closing it would leave an empty terminal area inside a still-open tab, which is exactly why korTTY's own "Close split" menu item is greyed out in that case. Close the tab yourself.

The threat model is a local process running as you, while the API is on. Such a process KTPH000canKTPH001 enumerate your windows, read any pane, type into any pane including submitting commands, open a tab for a saved connection, split a local shell, close a split pane, drive a detected coding agent, and raise a notification.
reach anything before you tick the box, or at all when enterprise policy denies the feature;
open a new window, or a tab for anything but a saved or teamwork connection: KTPH000 takes only the id or the name of one, and the policy still applies to it;
split anything other than a local shell, or split into a new connection;
close a tab, close korTTY's last pane, or rename a tab;
read or write your settings, your credentials, the vault, your SSH keys or the master password;
reach anything over the network — the listener is a unix socket or loopback, never anything else, and there is no setting that can widen it;
act without leaving an audit line, or without a desktop notification on its first write of the run.
Writes are not restricted to local shells — on purpose

Typing is allowed into remote panes too. Restricting it would break answering a coding agent that runs over SSH, and it would not be a real boundary anyway: a caller who can reach the socket can simply run KTPH000 in a local pane instead. The honest controls are the default-off switch, the policy deny, the audit line and the notification — not a filter that looks like a boundary and is not one.

A client can tell korTTY what kind of client it is with the optional KTPH000 parameter of KTPH001: KTPH002, the default, for KTPH003 and every script, or KTPH004 for an MCP server that passes korTTY on to an AI assistant. korTTY ships such a server itself: KTPH016KTPH005KTPH017. Any other value is refused with KTPH006. A connection that authenticated as KTPH007 stays an KTPH008 connection: a second KTPH009 on it as KTPH010 is refused with KTPH011. An KTPH012 client is served only while three things allow it: the Control API itself, the separate KTPH018MCP serverKTPH019 switch, which is off by default, and the KTPH020enterprise policyKTPH021 key KTPH013. When one of them says no, the handshake fails with KTPH014 or KTPH015, and the check is repeated before every request, so switching the MCP server off stops a connection that is already open at its next call.
An KTPH000 client gets a fixed, fail-closed list of methods:
KTPH000, KTPH001, KTPH002, KTPH003, KTPH004, KTPH005, KTPH006, KTPH007, KTPH008, KTPH009, KTPH010
Only with KTPH000Allow write toolsKTPH001, also off by default
everything else: events, focusing, splitting and closing, notifications, every KTPH000 method that acts, the reserved verbs, and any method a later korTTY adds until it is reviewed for MCP clients

A refused method answers KTPH000, with KTPH001 set to KTPH002 or KTPH003. The method list in the KTPH004 reply and the KTPH005 document show an KTPH006 client only the methods it may call, and the KTPH007 reply says in KTPH008 whether the write tools are on.

Everything an KTPH000 client reads is masked, always, because its model usually runs in the cloud: korTTY treats it like a cloud AI profile, with no opt-out. The screen and scrollback of KTPH001, the matched line and screen of KTPH002, the evidence line and the process command line of KTPH003, KTPH004 and the agent inside a pane description, and the tab and window titles all lose the connection's password, the organisation's replacement rules from the KTPH006enterprise policyKTPH007 and well-known token formats such as cloud access keys, each replaced by KTPH005. A command line is masked too, because it can carry an API key. A secret that runs over the right edge of a full-width row into the next one is masked as well; those rows are then wrapped again at the pane width.

KTPH000 and KTPH001 give an KTPH002 client at most 2000 rows and 64,000 characters, the newest ones kept, and set KTPH003 when anything was left out; a KTPH004 client keeps the protocol's own limits. KTPH005 adds KTPH006, the number of secrets masked in what it returned. KTPH007 searches the masked text, so a pattern cannot confirm a guessed password by whether it matched. A KTPH008 client reads the raw text exactly as before.

When KTPH007Allow write toolsKTPH008 is on, korTTY still asks you before every write an KTPH000 client wants to make. KTPH001, KTPH002 and KTPH003 open a prompt in korTTY titled KTPH009MCP write requestKTPH010, under the header KTPH011An AI assistant wants to type into a terminalKTPH012. It shows the client's name, marked KTPH013Client (reported by the client)KTPH014 because nothing proves it; the action, KTPH015Type textKTPH016, KTPH017Run a commandKTPH018 or KTPH019Press keysKTPH020; the target pane with its tab title and host, under KTPH021Pane:KTPH022; whether the write submits a line, answered KTPH023Yes, it runs as soon as it arrivesKTPH024 or KTPH025NoKTPH026; and the exact text or key names. The prompt also warns that an AI assistant may be repeating text it read in a terminal or on a web page, and asks you to allow the write only if you would type it yourself. Control characters and invisible characters are shown as symbols, such as KTPH004 for a line break, KTPH005 for Escape and KTPH006 for a direction override, so nothing reaches the pane that you could not see.
Nothing; the call answers KTPH000 with KTPH001 KTPH002
KTPH000Allow for this pane in this sessionKTPH001
This write, and every later KTPH000 into the same pane from the same MCP server process without another question, as long as the text submits nothing

The third answer is offered only for KTPH000 whose text contains no line break and no other control character and does not set KTPH001. KTPH002, KTPH003 and any text that submits a line always ask, because one click must never let an assistant run whatever it wants afterwards. The session is the KTPH004 process: it sends a random KTPH005 id with every connection, so the answer lasts until the assistant's host stops that process or korTTY quits. A client that sends no KTPH006 keeps the answer for one connection only.

A prompt that is not answered within 60 seconds counts as Deny (KTPH000 KTPH001), and so does a korTTY that cannot show one (KTPH002). A narrower surface, not a sandbox

KTPH000 is declared by the client, not proven. The list limits what an MCP server exposes to an AI assistant; it does not protect korTTY from an assistant that can also run shell commands as you, because any program of yours can read the token and connect as KTPH001. Treat every MCP client as a cloud model and everything it reads from a terminal as untrusted text.

Every action the API takes writes exactly one line to korTTY's log, carrying KTPH003byte counts and shapes onlyKTPH004 — KTPH000, KTPH001, KTPH002 — never terminal text. The line goes to korTTY's log and only there — the API writes nothing into a tab's session journal.

The first time a program types into a pane, splits or closes a pane, or sends a prompt or keys to a coding agent during a korTTY run, you get one desktop notification titled KTPH000A local program is controlling this windowKTPH001. One, not one per keystroke: the point is that a takeover is never silent, not that it becomes noise you learn to dismiss. korTTY also logs a warning naming the endpoint whenever the listener starts.
Actions a coding agent performs through the API are logged distinguishably from the ones you trigger in the Coding Agents panel, so reading the log tells you which was which.
